Package dyntabs.ai.voice

Class VoiceConfig

java.lang.Object
dyntabs.ai.voice.VoiceConfig
public final class VoiceConfig extends Object
Immutable settings for the two voice directions — speech → text (transcription) and text → speech (synthesis).

The one idea that makes this "easy"

Voice settings inherit from your chat settings. If easyai.properties already configures a provider and key for EasyAI.chat(), then forListening() and forSpeaking() reuse that same provider, key and base URL — so adding voice to an app usually costs zero new configuration. You only write an easyai.stt.* or easyai.tts.* key when you want voice to differ from chat.

Resolution order (first non-null wins)

Where each value comes from
SettingListening (forListening())Speaking (forSpeaking())
providereasyai.stt.provider → easyai.provider → "openai" easyai.tts.provider → easyai.provider → "openai"
API keyeasyai.stt.api-key → easyai.api-key easyai.tts.api-key → easyai.api-key
base URLeasyai.stt.base-url → easyai.base-url easyai.tts.base-url → easyai.base-url
modeleasyai.stt.model-name → "whisper-1" easyai.tts.model-name → "tts-1"
extraeasyai.stt.language (ISO-639-1, optional) easyai.tts.voice → "alloy"

Choosing a model name

The defaults are OpenAI's own ("whisper-1", "tts-1"). Deliberately, nothing is guessed from the base URL. If you point the base URL at another OpenAI-compatible service, name its model explicitly — for Groq, for instance, easyai.stt.model-name=whisper-large-v3. A wrong model name fails loudly at the provider, which is easier to debug than a library quietly picking a different one.

Analogy: a household's utility accounts. The lights and the heating bill to the same account unless you deliberately open a second one — and nobody rewires the house to guess which supplier you meant.
